verdict.reasoning: Patient reports lip swelling after prawn soup and that it is worsening: "I ordered a prawn soup... my lips started feeling a little weird... now I feel that there is a swelling on my upper lip and it's kind of getting bigger... it feels like it's getting worse."

Timing and location are described: swelling began about 30 minutes after eating, at the left corner of the upper lip and increased. Quotes: "That was... around seven"; "must have been like, I don't know half an hour maybe"; "my lips started feeling a little weird just in the in the corner sort of on the left first"; "there is like a swelling on my, on my upper lip and it's kind of getting bigger."

She reports difficulty breathing and possible chest involvement, consistent with dyspnea/possible throat tightness: "Is there any feeling of swelling in in your throat, like your throat is closing up...?" Patient: "Yeah actually, I, I feel like I can't breathe that well right now" and "it just generally feels a little difficult, but yeah it might be, I'm not sure."
Patient explicitly states dizziness: "Ohh sorry, the swelling is getting, ohh my god..." and later "Ohh, I feel a little dizzy right now to be honest, ohh."
Patient states asthma as past medical history: "But I generally have asthma so, I took I, I take, ohh what's it called? Salbutamol inhalers?... I generally have asthma."

She confirms peanut allergy and a childhood severe reaction needing hospital care: "I have a peanut allergy as well, like always had it"; doctor asks about hospital visit for severe reaction, patient: "Yeah is that well I was like six or something... I think."

She recounts a similar episode a year ago after late-night Chinese food with swelling and breathing difficulty: "maybe, I remember like a year ago... late night kinda Chinese place... I've woke up the next morning quite swollen up and had also I, felt really bad and quite difficult breathing."

She uses Salbutamol and sometimes antihistamines but is unsure which: "I take... Salbutamol inhalers"; "Do you use antihistamines... ?" Patient: "Hmm, no. I, I got no I do sometimes but I don't know which ones."

Doctor explicitly suspects anaphylaxis after prawn exposure, with lip swelling, breathing difficulty, dizziness, and history of peanut allergy and asthma: "you could be going into what we say an a, an anaphylactic reaction" following prawn soup exposure; symptoms documented earlier include upper lip swelling, "I feel like I can't breathe that well," dizziness, and history of peanut allergy and asthma as quoted in prior items.

Asthma and only SABA use are documented: "I generally have asthma"; doctor: "And any other inhalers? Is it just the Salbutamol that you use? Any other brown inhalers?" Patient: "Ohh I, no I don't think so, no." This indicates only short-acting beta-agonist (Salbutamol) use.

Doctor advises ambulance (999), not being alone, and having mother call: "I think we need to call an ambulance"; "hang on the line, while I'll call the ambulance"; later: "So just call the ambulance make sure that person's with you till the ambulance comes"; "Mum, if you can call the uh nine nine , nine nine nine yeah, and say that your there is a suspected anaphylactic reaction."

Doctor advises taking any available antihistamine while waiting: "Could you ask the person whether they have any antihistamines around, in the interim, while we're waiting"; later: "All right, so straight away take the antihistamines in the meantime all right."

Urgent ED evaluation and potential need for injection (IM adrenaline) are implied: "we need to call an ambulance" and "we are worried about an anaphylactic reaction so you need go straight away" and earlier: "you might need an injection like what your mum's." In an anaphylaxis context this reasonably implies intramuscular adrenaline and monitoring in ED.

Post-discharge GP follow-up for injections (epinephrine autoinjector) is recommended; allergy testing is not mentioned. Quote: "after you come out from the hospital do give us a ring back we might need to sort you out, um, with your injections and things like that." No explicit mention of allergy referral/testing, so that part is an addition.

The doctor does not state a plan to review asthma control or inhaler use after ED visit. The only follow-up mentioned is: "after you come out from the hospital do give us a ring back we might need to sort you out, um, with your injections and things like that." Asthma review is not discussed.
